what_it_does: Running a large language model on a cloud GPU cluster is hard because cloud providers offer a messy mix of GPU types connected by slow, uneven networks — not the ultra-fast NVLink connections that research systems assume. ThunderServe is a scheduling and routing system that assigns the right kind of GPU to each phase of AI inference, figures out the best parallelism strategy for each group, and can adapt on the fly when machines fail or workloads shift, achieving up to 2.1x more throughput than the best existing system at the same dollar cost.
method_in_detail:
The idea. LLM inference has two very different phases. The prefill phase — processing the user's input prompt — is compute-heavy, benefiting from GPUs with lots of raw arithmetic power (like the A40 with 149.7 TFLOPS). The decode phase — generating tokens one by one — is memory-bandwidth-limited, so it benefits from GPUs that can read memory fast (like the 3090Ti at 1008 GB/s). On a heterogeneous cloud cluster you can exploit this mismatch by routing each phase to the GPU type that fits it best.

How it works. ThunderServe frames the deployment problem as two nested optimisation layers.

Upper level — group formation and phase assignment. Given a pool of, say, 32 GPUs of five different types, the system must decide which GPUs belong to the same model replica and whether each replica handles prefill or decode. This is formally equivalent to a job-shop scheduling problem (NP-hard), so ThunderServe uses tabu search — an iterative neighbourhood-search heuristic that remembers recently tried configurations to avoid revisiting them and keeps exploring outward until it converges. It starts from a clustering of GPUs by network proximity, then proposes neighbours by flipping which phase a group handles, splitting a group, merging two groups, or moving GPUs between groups.

Lower level — parallelism and request routing. Given fixed groups and phase assignments, ThunderServe enumerates combinations of tensor parallelism (splitting one layer across GPUs) and pipeline parallelism (assigning different layers to different GPUs), using dynamic programming to find the fastest inter-GPU communication path. It separately optimises prefill groups for minimum latency and decode groups for maximum throughput. Request routing between prefill and decode replicas is then solved as a linear-programming transportation problem that accounts for the actual network bandwidth between each pair of replicas.

KV cache compression. Moving the model's running notes (key-value cache) from the prefill replica to the decode replica is expensive over slow Ethernet. ThunderServe compresses these notes from 16-bit to 4-bit for transmission, then immediately decompresses them on arrival — so neither phase does any computation at low precision, keeping accuracy within 2% of full precision.

Lightweight rescheduling. When a GPU goes offline or the workload type shifts from short-prompt coding tasks to long-answer conversations, ThunderServe adjusts only the phase assignments and routing fractions — not the model weights or parallelism structure — completing the reschedule in about 13 seconds versus 157 seconds for a full restart.

The result. On a 32-GPU heterogeneous cloud cluster (A6000, A5000, A40, 3090Ti), ThunderServe achieves up to 2.1x higher throughput and up to 2.5x lower latency than the best comparable system at the same hourly cost.
